title: Nonverbal Robot Feedback for Human Teachers
extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a robot can improve human teaching by providing feedback during demonstration-based teaching, analogous to the nonverbal cues that human students give teachers. The core question is whether minimally disruptive feedback can help teachers better understand what a learner robot has inferred, choose better examples, and know when to stop teaching.

The proposed intervention is a form of robot feedback in which the learner predicts the teacher’s next action and communicates that prediction nonverbally, with confidence indicated by speed. The authors study this first theoretically using an algorithmic teaching model and then empirically in two user studies. One study used 87 Amazon Mechanical Turk participants teaching a virtual decluttering agent; the second used 17 university students teaching a PR2 robot with gaze-based feedback. The task involved teaching sorting rules for placing objects into bins, not K-12 instruction, but a human-to-robot teaching context.

Across both the simulation and user studies, feedback generally improved teachers’ mental models of the learner and changed teaching strategy. It improved learner performance when the learner had a biased prior but could learn the task, and it helped teachers recognize limitations when the learner could not fully learn the task. In the in-person study, gaze was only effective when participants understood it as feedback; otherwise, some interpreted it as acknowledgement or observation. The paper concludes that nonverbal robot feedback can make human teachers more effective, though the communicative meaning of gaze must be clear for it to work well.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical HRI study with both simulation and user studies, but it is not a K-12 or teacher-preparation intervention and lacks randomization to a full educational treatment comparison in authentic classroom settings. The evidence is useful but indirect for the requested education taxonomy, and the in-person sample is small.
impact_tier_rationale: The study suggests modest positive effects on teacher understanding and teaching effectiveness, but only in a narrow robot-learning task and only under some learner-model mismatch conditions. There is no direct evidence of classroom-scale or general educational impact, and no clear planning-speed improvement is reported.

interventions.use_case: nonverbal robot feedback during human teaching, where a PR2 or virtual avatar predicts the teacher’s next action and communicates its current belief via gaze or movement speed to improve teaching effectiveness

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that teacher-facing feedback improved teachers’ mental model of the learner and sometimes improved teaching strategy, but the benefit depended on whether the teacher understood the feedback and on the learner prior condition. In the online study with 87 AMT participants, feedback significantly reduced mental model discrepancy and improved learner performance in the biased-prior condition, but had no benefit in the uniform-prior condition and reduced performance in the missing-feature condition; in the in-person study with 17 users, the subset who understood gaze as feedback (G1, n=9) showed improved learning and tracking, while the others did not.
finding.measure: mental model discrepancy, teaching strategy proxies, learner performance, and subjective ratings of informative teaching / stopping / knowing / doesn’t know
finding.study_size: n=87 (AMT); n=17 (in-person PR2), with G1 n=9 and G2 n=8

finding.finding_summary: Feedback helped teachers judge when to stop teaching and better infer what the learner knew or did not know, which is an efficiency gain even when final performance did not improve. The paper reports significant reductions in mental model discrepancy and improved subjective ratings for stopping/knowing in multiple conditions, though it does not report planning-time savings or effect sizes for speed.
finding.measure: Likert ratings for ease of stopping teaching, knowing what the learner knows/doesn’t know, and teaching-sequence length
